section.title: Unless the Lord Builds the House
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents of Solomon, eighth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Solomon, the builder of the temple, confesses that every house, city, and family depends entirely on the LORD, not on anxious human effort.
section.thesis: All human labor, whether building a house, guarding a city, or raising children, is empty striving unless the LORD is its builder and giver, so His people are called to trust Him rather than toil anxiously, a truth ultimately fulfilled in Christ, who builds His church on a foundation no labor of man could lay.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the futility of anxious labor without the LORD, verses 1 to 2, and the blessing of children as a heritage from the LORD, verses 3 to 5.

units.label: Unless the LORD builds the house

verses.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain.
In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat, for He gives sleep to His beloved.

units.label: Children are a heritage from the LORD

verses.text: Children are indeed a {{nachalah|heritage}} from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are children born in one's youth.
Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate.

nachalah.gloss: An inheritance or possession assigned as a lasting portion; children are called this, a heritage from the LORD given as a gift and reward, not a burden earned by effort.

basic.context: Attributed to Solomon, the builder of Israel's temple and fortifications, this Song of Ascents confesses that every human labor, house building, city guarding, and anxious toil, is empty unless the LORD is behind it, then turns to celebrate children as His good gift.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes the futility of self-reliant labor and the blessing of a full household, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern working diligently while trusting the LORD for the outcome, resting from anxious toil, and receiving children as His gift rather than a mere accomplishment.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm's key term is shav, vain or empty, repeated three times in verses 1 to 2 to hammer home the futility of labor without the LORD, before turning to nachalah, heritage, the gift-language used for children in verse 3.
basic.typology: The LORD as the true builder of the house anticipates Christ, who alone builds His church on an unshakeable foundation, and the children who defend their father at the gate anticipate believers who stand for Christ, the greater builder, against every opposing power.
basic.christ: Jesus declares, 'I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it,' Matthew 16:18, directly echoing this psalm's confession that only the LORD's building endures, and He is Himself the wisdom by which every truly lasting house, family, and city is established, 1 Corinthians 3:11.
basic.god: The LORD alone makes any labor fruitful, whether building, guarding, or working for daily bread, and He is the one who gives children as a heritage and reward, gifts that bring security and honor to those who receive them from His hand rather than seize them by anxious striving.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 16:18 shows Christ as the builder whose church the gates of Hades cannot overcome. Hebrews 3:3-4 honors Christ above every human builder, since the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself, and God is the builder of all things. Ephesians 2:19-22 pictures believers built together into a dwelling place for God.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's confession that only the LORD's building endures is fulfilled in Christ, who builds His church on a foundation no human effort could lay, and gives His people, like children in a household, both security and purpose in Him.

context.literary:
The psalm is two proverbs held together by one root. In Hebrew the verb 'build' is banah, the word for 'house' is bayit, and the word for 'sons' is banim. The first half of the psalm is about building a house, the second is about the sons who carry a house forward, and the shared consonants make the link audible. Whoever hears the psalm sung hears that a house is made of sons as well as stones, and that both are the LORD's building.

The opening is a triple repetition. 'In vain' marks the builders in verse 1, the watchmen in verse 1, and the early risers in verse 2. The first two are conditions, 'unless the LORD builds', 'unless the LORD protects', and the third is a plain statement. The effect is a ladder of three human efforts, construction, security and income, each declared empty without God. Verse 2 then closes on a contrast that is nearly a joke: while you toil for bread and lose sleep over it, He gives sleep to His beloved.

The second half is a different kind of poetry. Verses 3 to 5 are a string of images, a heritage, a reward, arrows, a quiver, and a blessing of the full quiver in verse 5. The tone changes from warning to benediction. The word 'blessed' in verse 5 is the same word that opens Psalm 1 and appears at the head of the next psalm, so this is the central hinge of a pair: Psalm 127 shows the gift, Psalm 128 shows the flourishing household.

The superscription names Solomon, and many readers connect that with the first half. A man who built the LORD's house and his own palace is the one who writes that all building is in vain without the LORD. The psalm's final scene is a gate, a public place of law and trade where a man defends his name. A reader who has followed the psalm from builders to bread to sons ends at the gate, where those sons stand beside their father.
context.historical:
The title 'of Solomon' makes this the only Song of Ascents attributed to him. Solomon built the temple, which took seven years, and his own house and a string of cities, 1 Kings 6:1 and 2, 1 Kings 9:1. He knew what building cost. Yet the LORD told him, once the temple was complete, that a kingdom built on stone alone would not last. If he or his sons turned away, the LORD would cut Israel from the land and cast the temple out of His sight, 1 Kings 9:6 to 9. The psalm reads as a principle learned at the end of that story, or as a warning given at its start.

David's own history sits under it. David once meant to build a house for the LORD, and the LORD answered through Nathan that He would build a house for David, 2 Samuel 7:11 and 27. The word 'house' there means a dynasty. In Psalm 127 the same double meaning, house as building and house as family, runs through verses 1 to 5. The LORD is the one who makes the house in both senses.

A city in this world was guarded by watchmen on the walls through the night, and a household lived by the daily labour of its head. Both are in view. The 'gate' in verse 5 was the place where a town's elders sat to settle disputes, Ruth 4:1 and 2. A father with many grown sons at the gate had witnesses, defenders and labourers, and in a world without police or a safety net, children were a family's security. That is the force of the arrow and the quiver. The warrior's weapons are what stand between his household and an enemy.

Nothing in the setting suggests the psalm is hostile to work. Israel was a farming people for whom early rising and long days were the way of life. The psalm does not tell anyone to stop. It tells them who gives the work its outcome. Sung by pilgrims going up to the city, it reminds them that the Zion they climb toward is guarded by the LORD, and that the heritage they bring with them, their families, is His gift.
context.canonical:
The psalm distils a conviction found across Scripture's wisdom writing. 'The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it', Proverbs 10:22. 'By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established', Proverbs 24:3. Ecclesiastes presses the other side, the toil that brings no rest, 'even at night, his mind does not rest', Ecclesiastes 2:23, and Ecclesiastes 5:12 observes that the sleep of the worker is sweet. The psalm names the source of the sweetness the Preacher can only observe.

The theme of sleep as trust runs through the Psalter. 'I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me', Psalm 3:5, and 'I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety', Psalm 4:8. Psalm 121, an earlier pilgrim song, calls the LORD the keeper who 'will neither slumber nor sleep', Psalm 121:4. The watchman of Psalm 127:1 and the keeper of Psalm 121 are the same office, and the psalm says only the second one actually keeps the city.

Children as a gift is a thread from Genesis on. God's first word to humanity is to be fruitful, Genesis 1:28; Rachel and Hannah are the wounded witnesses of how much the gift is wanted, Genesis 30:1 and 1 Samuel 1:10, and Psalm 113:9 sings of the barren woman made a joyful mother.

In the New Testament the language of building moves to the church. Jesus says 'I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it', Matthew 16:18. Paul writes 'You are God's field, God's building' and insists that the foundation is Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:9 to 11. Ephesians 2:20 to 22 describes the household being fitted together into a dwelling place for God, and 1 Peter 2:5 calls believers living stones. Hebrews 3:3 and 4 reads the verse behind the verse: every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm is written to men and women who are tired. The first hearers were builders, soldiers on watch, farmers and parents, many of them working hard and sleeping badly. The author wants to free them from the idea that the outcome rests on their effort alone. He does it with a deliberately blunt triple 'in vain', and then with the gentle reversal in verse 2, where God is shown giving rest to His beloved.

This is not an argument against diligence. Everything in the opening verses assumes that builders build and watchmen watch. It is an argument against anxious self-reliance, the sort of work that cannot stop because it has no one behind it. The psalm lets the worker put the tools down at night, because the real guarding and the real building are the LORD's.

The second half teaches that the most precious things in a household cannot be manufactured. Children are called a heritage and a reward, words that belong to the vocabulary of gift and of land. A father who has sons at the gate does not stand there because he earned them. The author wants the hearer to receive family with gratitude, and to see even the strength of the next generation as part of the LORD's building of the house he opened with.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 3 to 5 describe how an ancient household thought about children, and they do so with images of a warrior's quiver that belong to their own world. The psalm does not issue a command about the number of children a family should have. It says that children are a blessing and that a man with many has no reason to be ashamed. To treat 'a full quiver' as a rule, or as a measure of faith, goes beyond what is written.

The same care applies to verse 2. The psalm does not say that rest is earned by trust, or that those who lie awake are faithless. It describes the LORD as the one who gives rest to those He loves, and it invites trust. Anxious sleeplessness is not a sin, and the psalm is no weapon against the weary. It is a word of comfort offered to them.

What carries forward is the pattern: do the work in front of you, and let the LORD be the one who builds and guards. The prescription is a way of working, not a method of getting results.

debates.question: What does it mean that the LORD 'gives sleep to His beloved'?

views.label: The LORD gives rest as a gift
views.case: The most natural reading takes sleep as the object. The contrast with toiling for bread is exact: the one who trusts receives rest while the anxious worker does not. Psalm 3:5 and 4:8 use sleep in the same way, as the mark of someone whom the LORD sustains.

views.label: The LORD gives to His beloved while they sleep
views.case: The Hebrew can be read with sleep as the circumstance rather than the gift, 'He gives to His beloved in their sleep'. This reading is old, and some translations follow it. It would mean that the LORD's gifts come without the beloved's toil, even while they are unconscious.

debates.bearing: Both readings say the same thing about trust. The BSB takes sleep as the gift, and that fits the contrast. The second reading adds that what the beloved receive does not depend on their wakefulness. In either case the name 'beloved' is the reason, and it recalls that Solomon's own name from the LORD was Jedidiah, 2 Samuel 12:25.

debates.question: Is the 'full quiver' a promise or a general observation?

views.label: A proverb about the ordinary blessing of children
views.case: The imagery is of a warrior and his arrows, a proverb-style picture. Proverbs describe how God's world normally works and do not guarantee results in every case, as Scripture shows by recording barrenness and loss, Genesis 30:1 and 1 Samuel 1:10. Verse 5 says the man will not be put to shame, which is a statement about honour, not an entitlement.

views.label: A promise that applies to every faithful family
views.case: Some read it as a standing assurance that God grants children to those who trust Him. The language 'reward' and 'heritage' suggests direct divine giving. A reading of this kind would hold that the gift is the LORD's, so its absence calls for prayer.

debates.bearing: The harder reading is the first. Scripture makes children a gift, and gifts are God's to give or withhold. It never makes them a payment, and it comforts the childless elsewhere, Isaiah 54:1 and 56:4 and 5, and Psalm 113:9. The proverb teaches gratitude for the gift and honour for those who have it, without judging those who do not.

study.originalLanguages:
The word shav, 'vain' or 'empty', is the heart of verses 1 and 2. It means unreality, nothingness: what is done to no purpose. It is the same word used in the third commandment for taking the LORD's name 'in vain', Exodus 20:7. Here it describes work that produces nothing lasting. The repetition three times in two verses is a rhythm like a hammer. The Hebrew phrasing places it before the verb in each case and gives it the force of 'for nothing do the builders labour'.

The wordplay on banah, 'to build', and the nouns bayit, 'house', and banim, 'sons', has already been noted. It is worth seeing how the logic of the psalm depends on it. In the Old Testament 'to build a house' can mean to produce descendants, and a woman may be said to 'build' a household, Ruth 4:11 and Proverbs 14:1. When the LORD tells David 'I will build a house for you', 2 Samuel 7:27, the sense is a dynasty. Psalm 127 puts both senses in one hearing.

The verb in the second clause of verse 1, shamar, 'to guard' or 'keep', is the word used for the LORD in Psalm 121:3 to 5, where the keeper does not slumber. The city's human guards are shomrim, and the psalm says their guarding is in vain unless the LORD is the shomer. A reader who has just sung Psalm 121 will hear the echo.

The word 'beloved' in verse 2 is the noun yadid, from a root of affection, and it carries the sense 'dear one'. It is the same root as Jedidiah, the name Nathan gave Solomon, 2 Samuel 12:25. A psalm attributed to Solomon thus names the sleeper with the word his own name was made of. Elsewhere Moses uses it of Benjamin, 'the beloved of the LORD', who rests secure upon His shoulders, Deuteronomy 33:12. It is the language of safe rest.

In verse 3 'heritage' is nachalah, an allotment, the word used of the land given to each tribe and family, and of Israel as the LORD's own possession. Children are put in the category of land, the thing that cannot be earned and passes from God's hand into one's own. Alongside it stands sachar, 'reward' or 'wages', and 'the fruit of the womb'. The three terms say gift, payment and produce, all in the LORD's hand.

In verse 5 the BSB says the man 'confronts' the enemies at the gate, where the Hebrew verb is the common one for speaking, in a stem that can mean to speak with, argue with or address. The scene is a legal and civic encounter before a public gate, not a battle, and the 'arrows' are a family's weight of presence and testimony.

typology.type: The house built by the LORD, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The house the LORD builds is a house in two senses, a dwelling and a dynasty. Solomon's temple is a type: the LORD's name was placed in it, 1 Kings 9:3, but a house of stone needed more. In Christ both senses are fulfilled. He builds His church, Matthew 16:18, and He is the one in whom the whole building is fitted together into a holy temple, Ephesians 2:21. He is also the descendant of David whose house and kingdom the LORD establishes forever, 2 Samuel 7:13. The type falls short because Solomon's building could be laid waste and Christ's cannot, since the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.

typology.type: The sleep given to the beloved, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The rest the LORD gives is a pattern of the greater rest for which the first one points. Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28, and Hebrews describes a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9 and 10. He is also the Beloved Himself, the Son in whom the Father is well pleased, Matthew 3:17, and believers are given a place in that love, Ephesians 1:6. The type is limited because ordinary sleep ends in the morning, whereas the rest in Christ is the end of striving for acceptance.

typology.type: The sons at the gate, verses 4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: The father who is not put to shame before his enemies is a pattern of the people who belong to the Son, for 'Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame', Romans 10:11. He brings many sons to glory, Hebrews 2:10, and says 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me', Hebrews 2:13. The type breaks down at the point of origin: these children are not produced by a father's strength but are given, and they are His by redemption, not by birth.

A warrior's arrows are the weapons he puts into the field. In the New Testament God's people are sent out, Matthew 10:16, and Paul speaks of weapons that are not of the flesh but have divine power to demolish strongholds, 2 Corinthians 10:4. Christ's servants fight differently, with truth and the word of God, Ephesians 6:17. The type is partial because a quiver of arrows is spent and gone when it is shot, whereas those who go out in Christ's name are held in His hand, John 10:28.

study.christ:
The psalm's first verse is a statement Jesus makes true by what He does. 'I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it', Matthew 16:18. The words 'I will build' put the Son in the place the psalm gives to the LORD. The builders of the church, the apostles and the elders, are real, but Paul says plainly that the foundation is Jesus Christ and no one can lay another, 1 Corinthians 3:11. What the psalm says of the LORD, the New Testament says of the Son.

Hebrews takes the house idea further. 'Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself', Hebrews 3:3. The writer then adds that 'every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything', Hebrews 3:4. He uses the psalm's own logic to say that the one who built the house has more honour than the house, and applies it to Christ. Jesus is Solomon's greater Son, the one who builds a greater house, Matthew 12:42.

The sleep of verse 2 meets Him in two places. Jesus invites the weary to Himself for rest, Matthew 11:28, and He is Himself found asleep in a boat in a storm while His disciples panic, Mark 4:38. The Son sleeps untroubled in the storm, and when He is woken He rises and speaks, and the wind falls. In Him the psalm's picture of the beloved at rest becomes visible.

The beloved is the title that fits Him most exactly. At the Jordan the Father says, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased', Matthew 3:17. The psalm says the LORD gives to His beloved, and the Father has given the Son everything, John 3:35. It is in Him that believers are called beloved, Ephesians 1:6, and they receive from the Father what the Son receives.

The children of verses 3 to 5 find an answer in Hebrews 2. Christ is the pioneer who brings many sons to glory, Hebrews 2:10, and He says 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me', Hebrews 2:13. They are a heritage and a reward, given by the Father to the Son, and they come to Him as a gift.

The caution is that the psalm is not a hidden prediction of Jesus. It does not mention a Messiah, and the family language is about families. The connections here rest on how the New Testament itself uses the images of building, rest, and sons, and the psalm's central lesson, that the LORD alone builds, is the lesson of the cross: the church is not an achievement of its builders but a work of the Son.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm teaches about God is that He is the builder and the guard. Both words are active. The LORD is not a distant approver of human projects; He is the one who makes the house stand and keeps the city safe. The psalm assumes that human work is real and that God's work is more real. The opening conditions, 'unless the LORD builds', are the language of someone who knows how things fall apart without Him.

He is a God who gives rest. The verse is startling in a world where gods were thought to demand constant service. The LORD of Israel does not need anything from His servants, and He gives sleep to those He loves. The Psalter develops the idea, with the LORD as the keeper who does not sleep so that His people can, Psalm 121:4. He stays awake in order that they may lie down in peace, Psalm 4:8.

He is a God who gives. Children are a heritage and a reward, language that places them in the category of gift. The psalm does not say that they are earned by faithfulness, and the rest of Scripture is firm that He is free to give or withhold. Even when He withholds, He remains the one who settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother, Psalm 113:9, and the one who gives a name better than sons to the faithful eunuch, Isaiah 56:5. He is generous in His own ways.

He is also a God who loves. The word 'beloved' is not merely an affectionate adjective. It is the reason the sleeper sleeps. The ground of the rest is not the strength of the worker but the love of the one who watches. That is why the psalm is a comfort rather than a rebuke.

The psalm also holds two things together that people commonly set against each other, the sovereignty of God and the responsibility of people. The builders do build, the watchmen do watch, and the farmers do rise early. The psalm does not say that work is useless in itself. It says that it is useless as an independent source of security. That is the shape of providence across the Bible, where the LORD works in and through the work of His people, Philippians 2:12 and 13.

For worship the psalm teaches us to confess dependence in the middle of ordinary life. A prayer before work, a prayer at the close of a day, and a thank-you for a child are all ways of saying the psalm. It teaches the church to hold its building programmes, its security and its families open-handed, and to lie down without fear, because the LORD does not sleep.

crossReferences.note: David wanted to build a house for the LORD, and the LORD answered that He Himself would establish a house for David, and that David's descendant would build a house for His Name. The word 'house' carries both senses, which is the logic of Psalm 127:1 and the meaning of Solomon's name on the psalm.

After Solomon finished the temple the LORD told him that the house would stand only if he and his sons walked before Him. If they turned away, it would become a heap of rubble. It is the historical form of the warning in Psalm 127:1: a house that the LORD does not guard cannot be kept.

The LORD, Israel's keeper, neither slumbers nor sleeps. Read beside Psalm 127, it explains why the watchman's vigil is in vain without Him and why the beloved can sleep: One who never closes His eyes is keeping watch over them.

A person who trusts the LORD can lie down and sleep in peace, because the LORD alone makes him dwell in safety. It states from the sleeper's side what Psalm 127:2 states from God's: rest in the night is a sign of trust and a gift from the one who keeps the sleeper.

The Preacher describes a man whose days are grief and whose task is sorrow, who cannot rest even at night. This is the condition of verse 2's anxious toil, and the psalm answers it. What Ecclesiastes lays bare as futile, Psalm 127 sets under the care of the LORD.

By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established. Wisdom literature celebrates the building of a household, and Psalm 127 supplies the foundation under it: wisdom works, but the LORD is the one who builds. The two are not rivals, since wisdom is the way of working that depends on Him.

The LORD settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother of children. It confirms that children are His gift to give, and it shows that He gives them to those who had none, which is a necessary counterweight to a reading of Psalm 127 that sounds like a reward for the fortunate.

Jesus says 'I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it'. He takes the psalm's builder's role onto Himself and promises a house that no enemy at the gate can overthrow. It is the surest New Testament link to the first verse.

Paul tells the Corinthians they are God's field and God's building. He is an expert builder who laid a foundation, and others build on it, but no one can lay another foundation than Jesus Christ. It is the apostolic version of 'unless the LORD builds', applied to the work of the church.

The builder of a house has greater honour than the house itself, and God is the builder of everything. Hebrews uses the same reasoning as Psalm 127 to place Christ above Moses: He is the builder, and Moses is a servant in the house.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is about a house that God builds. In Genesis He builds a world and puts a man and a woman in it, with the task of filling it, Genesis 1:28. When that world is spoiled the LORD does not abandon the project. He builds a family out of Abraham, a nation out of Israel and a sanctuary in the wilderness that He fills with His glory, Exodus 40:34. Psalm 127 is a psalm for the long middle of this story, in which people build and guard and raise children inside the larger building that God is making.

The psalm answers a question left open since Babel, where humanity built for its own name, and the LORD scattered the builders, Genesis 11:4 to 8. Human buildings without God are the old story of vain labour. The psalm names that pattern and replaces it with a house that rests on His work. It also answers the curse in Genesis 3 on a man's labour: the toil and sweat of the ground, Genesis 3:17 to 19, remains, but the psalm gives the toiler a reason to rest.

The story narrows in David and Solomon. David's wish to build is turned into the LORD's promise to build for him, 2 Samuel 7. Solomon builds, and the building is destroyed by the exile, which is the psalm's warning made historical. Even so, the prophets promise a builder, 'the Branch', who will build the temple of the LORD, Zechariah 6:12 and 13.

In Christ the promise is kept. He builds His church and lays the foundation Himself, Matthew 16:18 and 1 Corinthians 3:11. His people are living stones, 1 Peter 2:5, and a family of sons, Hebrews 2:10 to 13. Their work for Him is not in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58, because it is done in the Lord, and they are free to rest in Him.

The new creation is the finished house. John sees the holy city come down from heaven, Revelation 21:2, and the LORD dwelling with His people, Revelation 21:3. The city needs no watchmen, because its gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25, and no enemy enters. The sleep of the beloved becomes the rest of those who no longer toil, Revelation 14:13, and every son and daughter given by the Father stands in His presence, with no shame at the gate.

sermon.title: Don't Eat the Bread of Anxious Toil
sermon.why: Piper expounds Psalm 127:1-2 directly, showing how trusting that the LORD builds the house frees believers from the anxious toil this psalm warns against.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say happens to builders and watchmen if the LORD is not in their labor?

options.text: Their building and guarding are done in vain.
options.note: This is the psalm's exact double claim, that labor without the LORD is empty.

options.text: They succeed even more quickly than expected.
options.note: The psalm states the opposite, that such labor is futile, not accelerated success.

options.text: They receive a smaller reward but still succeed.
options.note: The text says the labor is in vain, not merely reduced in reward.

options.text: They are guaranteed eventual success after delay.
options.note: The psalm gives no such guarantee apart from the LORD's involvement; it declares the labor vain.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, what does the LORD give to His beloved?

options.text: Sleep, in contrast to anxious, exhausting toil.
options.note: This is the specific gift named in verse 2, contrasted with rising early and staying up late in anxious labor.

options.text: Unlimited wealth regardless of effort.
options.note: The verse speaks of sleep and rest, not a promise of unlimited wealth.

options.text: A guarantee of never needing to work again.
options.note: The psalm assumes ongoing labor; it contrasts anxious toil with trust, not labor with idleness.

options.text: Extra hours added to each day.
options.note: The text speaks of sleep and rest given by God, not literally extended days.

options.text: As a heritage from the LORD and the fruit of the womb as His reward.
options.note: This is the psalm's exact, positive description of children as a divine gift.

options.text: As a burden to be endured for the family's sake.
options.note: The psalm frames children as a gift and reward, the opposite of a mere burden.

options.text: As a sign of excessive wealth.
options.note: The text ties children to the LORD's gift and reward, not to wealth as such.

options.text: As a purely private matter with no wider significance.
options.note: Verse 5 gives children public significance, standing with their father at the gate.

quiz.q: What image does verse 4 use to describe children born in one's youth?

options.text: Arrows in the hand of a warrior.
options.note: This is the exact image the psalm uses, picturing strength and purposeful defense.

options.text: Seeds scattered without purpose.
options.note: The image given is purposeful and strong, arrows in a warrior's hand, not aimless scattering.

options.text: Coins stored in a treasury.
options.note: The psalm's image is about strength and defense, not stored wealth.

options.text: Birds flying freely without direction.
options.note: The specific image is arrows aimed with purpose, not birds in flight.

quiz.q: How does Jesus echo this psalm's confession that only the LORD's building endures?

options.text: He declares He will build His church so that the gates of Hades cannot overpower it.
options.note: Matthew 16:18 is the direct New Testament fulfillment of this psalm's confession.

options.text: He teaches that human builders never need divine help.
options.note: This directly contradicts the psalm's and Jesus's own teaching on dependence on God.

options.text: He applies the psalm only to physical construction projects.
options.note: Jesus applies the building imagery to His church, a spiritual house, not merely physical construction.

options.text: He rejects the psalm's imagery as outdated.
options.note: Jesus draws directly on this very imagery rather than rejecting it.

questions: The psalm names three kinds of labor, building, guarding, and toiling for bread, all empty without the LORD. Where in your own work are you laboring anxiously as if it all depended on you?
Verse 2 contrasts anxious toil with the rest the LORD gives His beloved. What would it look like for you to work diligently but rest from anxiety this week?
Children are called a heritage and reward from the LORD, not merely an achievement or burden. How does this shape the way you view family, whether your own children or those in your life?

The image of arrows in a warrior's hand suggests children are shaped with purpose and aim. How are you intentionally aiming the next generation, whether your own children or those you mentor, toward Christ?

Jesus declares He will build His church so that nothing can overpower it. Where do you need to trust Christ as the builder rather than relying on your own strength to sustain your ministry, family, or work?

translationNotes.note: For He gives sleep to His beloved can also be rendered He gives to His beloved in sleep, meaning God accomplishes good for His people even while they rest, without their frantic effort; both readings teach the same trust.
Heritage, nachalah, is inheritance language elsewhere used for the land itself, Numbers 26:53, applying the same gift-language of a lasting, God-given portion to children.
The gate was the ancient city's place of legal and civic business; a man supported by many grown children could face disputes there without fear of being overwhelmed or shamed.
